title: Creating and Using Multiple Objects
summary: Remove the #1 beginner doubt: 'If I write one class, can I make multiple objects?' Discover how independent objects live peacefully without mixing up their data.
learningObjectives: Instantiate multiple independent objects from the same class blueprint
Understand that each object has its own separate copy of instance variables
Predict program outputs when manipulating several objects in sequence
expectedOutcomes: Total confidence that modifying object A will never accidentally alter object B
Ability to build small multi-entity programs without confusion

activities.title: Three Houses on the Same Street

analogy.headline: House #1 paints their door red. Does House #2's door turn red?
analogy.story:
Imagine a suburban street where 3 houses were built from the exact same architectural floor plan.

- The owner of House #1 paints their front door **Bright Red**.
- The owner of House #2 paints their door **Sky Blue**.
- The owner of House #3 paints their door **Forest Green**.

Does painting House #1's door suddenly change House #2's door? Of course not! Even though both houses share the exact same floor plan (the class), each house is an independent physical structure with its own walls and its own door.

In Java, `student1`, `student2`, and `student3` are those three houses. Each holds its own unique state in memory.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A class is written once. Every object you create from it gets its own completely independent set of variables.

activities.title: Independent State in Memory
Working with 3 Independent Students
activities.description: Each student object neatly manages its own name, age, and course. When you call s1.display(), it prints Rahul's details. When you call s2.display(), it prints Priya's details. Zero confusion, zero variable collision!

questions.prompt: If you have 'Student s1 = new Student();' and 'Student s2 = new Student();', how many copies of the 'name' field exist in memory?
options: Only 1 copy shared by both students
2 separate copies, one for s1 and one for s2
Zero copies until a method is called
questions.explanation: Each object instance receives its own separate set of instance variables. So s1 has its own 'name', and s2 has its own distinct 'name'.

hints.hint: Remember the three houses on the same street.

questions.prompt: How many objects can you create from a single Java class?
options: As many as needed, limited only by your computer's memory
Only as many as the number of methods in the class
questions.explanation: A class is a reusable blueprint. You can create 1, 100, or 1,000,000 objects from a single class!

hints.hint: How many cookies can you cut with one cookie cutter?

interviewQA.question: Do objects created from the same class share their instance variables?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. Each object created from a class possesses its own independent copy of instance variables. Modifying an instance variable on one object has no impact whatsoever on other objects created from that same class.
keyPoints: Each object instance holds its own independent state
Instance variables are allocated separately for each object
Allows safe concurrent modeling of multiple real-world entities
commonMistakes: Confusing instance variables with static variables (which are shared across all instances). Keep the answer focused on normal instance variables.

activities.title: Lesson 6 Checkpoint
checklist: I understand that creating multiple objects from one class creates multiple independent states.
I know that changing a field on s1 will never affect s2.
I can create 3 or more distinct objects and display their information cleanly.

practiceProblems.title: Manage Three Books in a Mini Library
practiceProblems.description:
Create a Book class with String title and String author. In Main, create 3 books:
1. 'Atomic Habits' by 'James Clear'
2. 'Clean Code' by 'Robert Martin'
3. 'Java Basics' by 'LearnBySelf'
Print each book on a new line in the format: '[title] by [author]'.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Atomic Habits by James Clear
Clean Code by Robert Martin
Java Basics by LearnBySelf
practiceProblems.hint: Create b1, b2, and b3 using new Book(), set their fields, and print them.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Instantiate 3 Book objects with different titles and authors, and print their details.
hints: Notice how each book retains its own title and author independently.

practiceProblems.title: Two Rectangles with Independent Dimensions
practiceProblems.description: Create a Rectangle class with int length and int width, and a method void printArea() that prints: 'Area: [length * width]'. In Main, create r1 (length 5, width 4) and r2 (length 10, width 3). Call printArea() on both.
practiceProblems.hint: Inside printArea(), compute: int area = length * width; System.out.println("Area: " + area);
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create two Rectangle objects with different dimensions and print their areas.
hints: Each rectangle calculates its own area using its own length and width.
